instructions: Fill a large pot with water, put it over low heat and let it come up to a gentle boil while you get everything else ready.
Peel and grate the ginger. That should be about 2 tsp. Mince the 4 garlic cloves.
Cut the 4 bok choy in half lengthwise. Rinse them well under cold water, getting between the leaves, and let them drain.
Make the sesame base. In a medium bowl, stir the 1/4 cup tahini and 2 tsp miso together until smooth, then whisk in 2 tbsp of the soy sauce and the 2 tsp rice vinegar.
Heat a medium saucepan over medium heat and add the 2 tbsp oil, then the 3/4 lb pork. Cook it, breaking it up with a spatula, until there's no pink left and the bits start to brown, about 6 minutes.
Add the 2 tbsp sake and stir. Add the ginger and garlic and stir for about 30 seconds, until they smell fragrant.
Stir in the 1 tbsp doubanjiang and the last 4 tsp soy sauce. Turn the heat to medium-low and cook for 2 to 3 minutes, until the liquid has almost cooked away. Take the pan off the heat.
Transfer half the pork into a small bowl and cover it to keep it warm. This is the topping.
Add the sesame base to the pork still in the saucepan, off the heat, and stir it through.
Put the saucepan back over medium heat. Pour in the 3 cups chicken stock a little at a time, stirring as you go, then the 3 cups soy milk the same way.
Add 1/2 tsp salt and taste it. It should taste a little salty on its own, so add a pinch more if it's flat. Turn the heat off and cover the pan.

Set a bowl of cold water by the stove. Turn the big pot up to high. Lower the bok choy in stem end first and cook for about 2 minutes, until the stems are tender. Lift it out into the cold water and keep the pot of water on the heat for the noodles.
Squeeze the water out of the bok choy and set it on a plate.
Warm the soup over medium heat until it's steaming. Don't let it boil, or the soy milk can split.
Loosen the 4 portions of noodles with your fingers. Cook them in the boiling water as the package says, usually 2 to 4 minutes, stirring with chopsticks so they don't stick together.
Drain the noodles well, shaking the strainer hard so no water ends up in the soup. Divide them among 4 deep bowls.
Taste the soup again. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Ladle the hot soup over the noodles and top each bowl with the reserved pork and two bok choy halves. Serve right away with the chili oil on the table.
method_notes: Both cook ground pork with ginger, garlic, doubanjiang and soy sauce until it's nearly dry, make a creamy broth from sesame paste and chicken stock, and top ramen with the pork and blanched greens. Just One Cookbook stirs a sesame and miso base into half the pork, then adds chicken stock and soy milk, with chili oil whisked into the base; No Recipes uses stock only, grinds toasted sesame seeds into the base, and marinates the topping pork in sweet bean sauce. This one follows Just One Cookbook with tahini, which it names as a swap for Japanese sesame paste, and to keep the base mild it uses half the lead's doubanjiang and moves the chili oil to the table.
